sections.heading: Replace the Three-Month Rule With a Risk Model
paragraphs: An emergency fund is not a badge earned by reaching one universal number. It is liquid money assigned to absorb an expense shock, an income shock or both. The right target depends on essential costs, income reliability, insurance and how quickly the household can adapt.

The opening photograph shows a jar clearly labeled “Savings” because the first distinction must be visible: emergency cash is reserved, not merely whatever happens to remain in checking. The label needs written use rules as much as a separate container.

Job title alone cannot set the number. Two nurses, designers or drivers can have different hours, employers, contracts, health needs, dependents and alternative income. Use job characteristics rather than stereotypes about an occupation.

Start with three layers: an operating buffer for transaction timing, a starter reserve for a common urgent cost, and an income-replacement reserve measured against essential monthly burn. Each layer solves a different problem.

Treat “months” as a translation of dollars, not a savings product. If essential burn is $3,200, three months means $9,600. A household that cuts burn to $2,700 changes the runway without earning another dollar.
Use settled, accessible cash in the calculation. Credit limits, unvested equity, an expected bonus, possible severance and retirement balances are not equivalent to a liquid reserve.

A higher target is not always the next priority. Past-due housing, uninsured medical needs or very high-rate debt may need attention alongside a starter reserve. Sequence should reduce the greatest immediate harm.
Review the model after a job change, move, new dependent, health event, insurance change or major debt payoff. A fund sized for last year’s life can be too small or unnecessarily large today.

Keep the target honest about public support without assuming eligibility or timing. Unemployment insurance, disability coverage and family help can reduce a gap, but only confirmed rules belong in the base case.
The model succeeds when the household can explain the target in dollars, the risks it covers and the event that permits a withdrawal.

sections.heading: Calculate Essential Burn Before Choosing the Target
paragraphs: Essential burn is the lean monthly cost of keeping the household safe and able to earn. Include housing, basic utilities, food, transport, health care, insurance, childcare, minimum debt payments, taxes and essential connectivity.
Use actual statements, not a round estimate. Average variable costs across normal months and note seasonal peaks. Convert annual premiums, registration and professional fees into monthly equivalents.

Separate current spending from transition spending. Commuting may fall after job loss, while health insurance, job-search travel or childcare for interviews can rise. Model the change instead of deleting every work cost.

Create three columns: protected, reducible and pausable. Protected costs preserve housing, health and earning capacity. Reducible costs can step down after a trigger. Pausable items stop quickly without a contract penalty or serious loss.

Include minimum debt payments but show extra principal separately. During a disruption, the extra payment may pause while minimums and priority bills remain funded. Contact creditors before missing payments if cash becomes insufficient.

Add irregular essentials expected during the target period: vehicle maintenance, medication refill, deductible, school need or home repair. A monthly average may hide the cash date, so keep a calendar beside the budget.
If income is variable, calculate burn against a low-income month as well as zero income. A freelancer may need smoothing cash more often than complete income replacement.
Do not reduce food, medicine, heating or necessary care below a safe level to make runway look longer. A transition budget must be livable enough to execute for months.

For a multi-income household, calculate burn after each income disappears separately. Payroll deductions and employer health coverage can make the surviving net income different from a simple salary subtraction.
The burn number is ready when every line has a source, every annual cost has a payday share and another adult could run the household from it.

sections.heading: Separate Expense Shocks From Income Shocks
paragraphs: An expense shock is an urgent repair, medical bill, travel need or deductible. An income shock is reduced hours, delayed client payment, disability or job loss. One reserve can cover both, but the sizing logic differs.
Use the largest plausible near-term deductible or repair as the starter expense target. It need not cover every catastrophe; insurance, payment arrangements and public support can share larger risks.

Income replacement begins with essential burn multiplied by a chosen runway. Then subtract only reliable income that would continue, such as a spouse’s conservative net pay or a confirmed benefit estimate.

[[S1|CFPB guidance]] identifies car repairs, medical costs, home repairs and loss of income as common emergency-fund uses. It also emphasizes that fluctuating workers benefit from saving during stronger weeks or months.

A predictable annual bill is not an emergency. Hold insurance premiums, taxes, holidays and routine maintenance in sinking funds. Otherwise the emergency balance will appear to fail every time the calendar advances.
Create separate ledger labels even if all short-term savings sits in one account. The sum of emergency, annual-bill and other buckets must equal the actual account balance.
When one event combines both shocks—such as illness reducing work while creating medical costs—use the expense layer first and preserve income-replacement cash for recurring bills.
Insurance changes the tail risk, not every cash need. A deductible, waiting period, excluded service or reimbursement delay can still require liquid money.
Do not assume family help arrives on demand. If support is part of the plan, discuss amount, timing and whether it is a gift or loan before counting it as a secondary resource.
The two-shock framework prevents a $1,000 repair target from being mistaken for three months of runway, or a large runway target from delaying a useful starter cushion.

sections.heading: Score the Job by Income Reliability, Not Prestige
paragraphs: Use five factors: variation in hours or sales, likelihood of delayed payment, concentration in one employer or client, availability of similar work, and time required to replace benefits. Score each low, medium or high based on evidence.
A prestigious role can be concentrated and slow to replace; a modest role can have predictable demand and portable skills. Compensation level does not measure income reliability by itself.
Review the last twelve months of deposits. Count the lowest normal month, frequency of late payments, unpaid gaps and reliance on overtime. The bank record often reveals more than the job title.

Check the employment arrangement: at-will employee, fixed contract, union agreement, civil service, seasonal schedule, platform work or self-employment. Each has different protections and variability, but none guarantees income.
Estimate replacement time using recent openings, required licenses, location and hiring steps. A specialized role with few employers may need more runway even when current pay is stable.

Assess employer or client concentration. A contractor with ten recurring clients can be less exposed than one with a single large client. A household with two wages from the same employer or industry remains concentrated.
Include benefits concentration. Losing a job that supplies family health insurance can increase burn sharply. A second job without benefits may not replace the lost package.
Rate skill portability. Current credentials, references and a maintained portfolio can shorten a search. A lapsed license or highly company-specific skill can lengthen it.
Use the score to select a target range, then validate against dollars. Do not publish an exact formula that implies certainty a household does not have.
The score is useful when changing one risk factor—such as adding a client or spouse coverage—changes the rationale and potentially the target.

Re-score with evidence rather than anxiety. Note the date, source and reason for each rating, then review quarterly. A hiring freeze, lost client or expired credential may raise risk; a signed long-term contract, new portable skill or independent household income may lower it. Keep a range when evidence is mixed instead of forcing a false point estimate.

sections.heading: Size Stable Salaried and Dual-Income Households Carefully
paragraphs: A salaried worker with predictable hours, broad demand and portable benefits may choose a lower runway range than a worker with irregular income, but “salaried” does not mean protected from layoffs or illness.
Consider employer stability, probation, funding cycle and role concentration. A new salaried job can be less stable than a long-held hourly role with a union agreement.
Dual income reduces risk only when incomes are genuinely independent. Two people at the same company, in the same cyclical industry or dependent on the same childcare arrangement share exposure.

Model one-income survival. Subtract the lost worker’s net pay, add replacement health premiums or commute changes, and calculate the remaining monthly deficit. The fund needs to cover the deficit, not necessarily all household burn.
If either income alone covers essentials, the reserve can focus on deductibles, timing and the period before the household adjusts. Still maintain cash for simultaneous shocks.
Employer disability and paid leave can reduce an illness-related gap, but record waiting periods, benefit percentage, cap, tax treatment and eligibility. A policy summary is evidence; memory is not.
Keep professional search readiness current even for stable roles. Shorter replacement time can reduce the amount of income runway needed, though hiring outcomes are never guaranteed.
Households with strong family support should document what support means. Free housing is different from a possible short-term loan and may have personal constraints.
A stable household should not overfund cash indefinitely while neglecting retirement, high-rate debt or insured long-term goals. Set a ceiling and a review date.
The target fits when it covers the modeled deficit, benefit transition and plausible expense shock without assuming both incomes are invulnerable.

Test the plan against benefit loss as well as wages. If the lost job carries family health insurance, add the confirmed continuation or replacement premium and any deductible reset to the monthly deficit. If the surviving job provides coverage, record its special-enrollment deadline and payroll cost. The household may be income-diversified but benefit-concentrated.

sections.heading: Give Variable, Seasonal and Freelance Work More Smoothing Cash
paragraphs: The midpoint photograph shows a freelancer working on a laptop because irregular work changes the job of cash. The reserve must smooth ordinary lean periods as well as absorb true emergencies.

For hourly workers, compare scheduled minimum hours with actual hours across a year. Do not build fixed obligations from overtime or peak-season schedules. Save part of strong checks for known low-hour periods.
Seasonal workers should separate off-season living money from the emergency fund. The off-season is predictable and belongs in an income-smoothing bucket; emergencies can still occur during it.
Freelancers and contractors need a business buffer for software, insurance, subcontractors and slow invoices, plus a household reserve. Mixing both hides whether the business can pay itself.
Invoice timing matters as much as annual income. Record average days to payment, late-client concentration and the gap between completing work and receiving cash.
Self-employed workers also need a tax reserve. Estimated-tax money is not emergency savings. Keep it visibly separate and use current IRS guidance or qualified advice for obligations.

Platform and gig workers should include vehicle maintenance, fuel, commercial coverage, device replacement and platform access risk. Gross app earnings overstate household cash after operating costs and taxes.
Commission and tipped workers can use a conservative base drawn from low normal months. Apply a preset percentage of exceptional months to smoothing cash until the target is reached.

[[S2|FDIC guidance]] supports automatic saving and starting with any sustainable amount. For irregular income, a percentage transfer after each settled payment can adapt better than a fixed monthly draft.
The higher target is justified by payment variance and ordinary lean periods, not by a claim that freelance or hourly work is inherently inferior.

Calculate two balances separately on the dashboard: money for the expected lean season and money for events outside the expected pattern. When a slow month arrives on schedule, use smoothing cash. When illness, equipment failure or an exceptional client loss occurs, use the emergency tier. This separation shows whether pricing and annual income are sustainable. Use the strongest month to fill the predictable off-season bucket first, then add to the emergency tier. If every strong month is needed merely to survive the expected slow season, the issue may be pricing, fixed business costs or annual income rather than an undersized emergency fund. Revisit rates, capacity and recurring business commitments before raising household cash targets.

sections.heading: Adjust for Commission, Client and Business Concentration
paragraphs: A salesperson with a base salary and diversified accounts has a different profile from a commission-only worker dependent on one product cycle. Break compensation into guaranteed, variable and reimbursed components.
Do not count expense reimbursements as income. Restore the account that paid the business cost. Otherwise both earnings and available reserve are overstated.
For commission, measure the longest historical gap between meaningful payments and add the sales cycle for a replacement role. Pipeline value is not cash until the payment conditions are met.
A consultant should rank clients by share of net revenue, contract notice and payment history. Losing a client that provides 60 percent of income resembles a layoff more than routine churn.
Business owners need operating cash distinct from household emergency money. Payroll, sales tax, inventory and vendor obligations cannot be quietly assigned to the family reserve.
Check personal guarantees and business debt. A business interruption may create household claims beyond lost income. Qualified legal and accounting help can clarify exposure.
Build a client-diversification target alongside cash. One additional reliable payer can reduce concentration more efficiently than holding an indefinitely larger reserve.
Use contracts and invoice data rather than optimism. Renewal conversations, unsigned proposals and verbal commitments belong in contingent forecasts, not the base case.
When cash flow improves, refill smoothing and tax buckets before raising owner draws. A strong quarter does not establish a permanent monthly income.
The reserve target should fall only after concentration, payment timing or fixed costs truly improve—not merely after one unusually good month.

Add a payment-delay test to the target. Assume the largest client pays one full billing cycle late while ordinary business and household costs continue. Include collection time, platform payout holds and chargeback exposure where relevant. If that scenario consumes tax money or personal credit, increase business working capital, change invoice terms or reduce client concentration before calling the household reserve complete. Recheck the test after each major contract renewal, platform policy change, delayed invoice or suddenly lost client relationship entirely.

sections.heading: Account for Benefits, Dependents and Geographic Mobility
paragraphs: Job risk is only one side of the target. A household with dependents, ongoing treatment or limited mobility can need more time and cash even with stable employment.

Price health coverage alternatives before a loss. Compare employer continuation, a spouse’s plan, Marketplace coverage and public programs where eligible. Include premiums, deductibles, networks and timing.
Disability coverage can replace some income after a waiting period, subject to definitions and caps. Emergency cash must bridge the wait and cover costs the policy excludes.
Childcare may not disappear during unemployment because interviews, training and applications take time. Model a reduced but realistic amount rather than zero.
Caregiving obligations can limit location, schedule and job options. Replacement time should reflect the jobs the worker can actually accept.
Homeowners may face larger repair shocks; renters may face deposits and moving costs. Neither category automatically needs more cash without examining insurance, lease and property condition.
Geographic mobility can shorten a search but create relocation costs. A “move for work” backup needs deposits, travel and overlap, not just confidence that relocation is possible.
Visa, licensing and union rules can constrain replacement work and benefit access. Seek current official or qualified guidance; do not use a generic job-type table for legal status.
A household supporting relatives should identify which transfers are essential and what changes during a disruption. Unwritten obligations still affect runway.
The adjusted target reflects people and constraints, not just the worker’s paycheck.

Build a coverage bridge in dollars. List the last employer-covered day, first replacement day, full interim premium, prescriptions and appointments that cannot safely wait. A fund expressed only as months can miss a one-time premium or deductible. Health and disability needs should be documented without reducing necessary care to make the target look achievable.

sections.heading: Use Three Tiers Instead of One Intimidating Goal
paragraphs: Tier one is the operating buffer: cash in checking for timing errors and ordinary bill variation. Its target might be the largest variable bill or several days of essential spending.

Tier two is the starter emergency reserve: enough for a deductible, urgent repair or short income delay. CFPB materials often present $500 and then $1,000 as practical starting milestones while emphasizing that needs vary.
Tier three is income runway: essential burn multiplied by the risk-based number of months, adjusted for reliable continuing income. It grows after the first two tiers are functional.
Milestones create useful wins without pretending the final target is reached. Label progress as buffer funded, starter shock funded, one month funded and target range funded.
Do not invest tier-one or tier-two money in volatile assets. A market decline can arrive with job loss. Match risk and access to the emergency purpose.
Income runway can use more than one insured savings vehicle if access remains timely and penalties are understood. Avoid locking the entire reserve in a certificate with an early-withdrawal penalty.
Keep sinking funds outside the three tiers. Annual insurance, taxes and planned maintenance must not inflate emergency progress.
If the target seems impossible, automate a small transfer and assign part of windfalls or extra-paycheck months. Progress from zero to a starter reserve materially changes options.
After reaching the ceiling, redirect new saving to retirement, debt or another goal while preserving interest and periodic inflation updates.
The tier system works when each milestone has a distinct job and the account ledger agrees with real balances.

Set a funding order for each payday. Maintain the checking cushion, complete the starter reserve, fill predictable sinking funds due soon, then build income runway toward its range. When one tier is used, refill it before sending new money to a lower-priority goal. The order prevents one large target from obscuring immediate protection.

sections.heading: Store the Reserve for Access, Safety and Restraint
paragraphs: An emergency fund should be available quickly, protected from ordinary spending and not exposed to large market loss. An insured savings account often fits, subject to fees, ownership and coverage rules.

[[S3|The FDIC explains]] that deposit insurance applies by depositor, insured bank and ownership category under its rules. Credit unions may have NCUA insurance. Verify the institution and product rather than assuming every app balance is insured.
Compare annual yield only after checking monthly fees, minimums, transfer limits and access. A small yield difference is not worth an account that repeatedly charges fees or delays urgent money.

Keep a portion in the same institution as bills if transfer speed matters, and a portion elsewhere if separation reduces temptation or protects against one account outage. Complexity should serve a specific risk.

Do not keep a large household reserve as physical cash. Theft, fire and loss risk are substantial, and cash earns no interest. A modest emergency amount may be useful only within a broader safety plan.
Use multifactor authentication, unique passwords and transaction alerts. Secure recovery email and phone. The reserve is not resilient if a scammer can redirect it.
Name beneficiaries or payable-on-death arrangements where appropriate and understand account ownership. Emergency access for a partner should not depend on sharing passwords.
Test a small transfer before relying on a new account. Record routing, transfer timing and support contacts securely.
Keep the debit card out of the everyday wallet if that reduces impulse use, but know how to access funds during a true emergency.
The storage decision is complete when money can reach the bill on time, remains protected under verified terms and is inconvenient enough to discourage casual spending.

sections.heading: Balance High-Rate Debt Against Cash Resilience
paragraphs: High-rate debt and an empty reserve reinforce each other. Paying every dollar to debt can force the next repair back onto the card; saving indefinitely while paying extreme interest can also be costly.
Begin with a starter reserve while keeping minimums current. Then direct extra cash based on interest rate, delinquency consequences, job risk and access to alternatives.
Compare guaranteed interest cost with the value of liquidity, not with expected investment returns. The decision is about debt and cash, not speculative arbitrage.
Priority arrears, secured debt and essential services can outrank both extra saving and unsecured acceleration. Seek reputable counseling when minimums and necessities cannot fit together.
Do not treat a credit line as the fund. Lenders can reduce limits, cards can fail and borrowing creates future payments during the income shock.
After a balance is repaid, redirect its former payment automatically to the reserve until the target is restored. This uses existing cash flow rather than finding new money.
If employment risk rises sharply, temporarily favoring liquidity can be reasonable, but document the trigger and review date. Fear should not become a permanent excuse to ignore expensive debt.
Employer retirement matching may still deserve a place if affordable. Giving up match to overfund cash has an opportunity cost; taking on debt to capture it is also problematic.
Keep debt-payoff and reserve balances on one dashboard. A rising savings account alongside unchanged revolving debt may hide a deteriorating net position.
The balance is successful when a common shock does not recreate the debt and the interest burden still declines on a deliberate schedule.

sections.heading: Write Withdrawal and Refill Rules Before the Crisis
paragraphs: Define an emergency as necessary, urgent and unplanned, or as a documented income gap. Examples can include essential repair, deductible, medical travel or core bills after lost work.
Routine maintenance, holidays and known annual premiums belong in sinking funds. A sale, vacation or upgrade is not an emergency because it has a deadline.
Allow judgment. A rigid list cannot anticipate every health, safety or family event. Require a short note: what happened, amount, alternative considered and refill start date.
Use the smallest appropriate tier. Timing errors come from the operating buffer; repairs use the starter reserve; recurring bills during job loss use runway.
Do not borrow at high cost to preserve a symbolic savings balance. The fund exists to be used for qualifying events. Using it successfully is not failure.
After withdrawal, recalculate remaining months. Pause lower-priority contributions and activate the refill rule on the next stable payday.
If income remains disrupted, do not demand immediate refill. Preserve essentials, use benefits and provider hardship options, and update the transition budget.
Review what the event taught. A recurring repair may belong in maintenance; an insurance exclusion may require coverage review; a delayed invoice may require different business terms.
Households should agree who can authorize transfers and how to communicate. Do not make urgent medical or safety access depend on one unavailable person.
The rules are effective when they permit confident use, prevent routine leakage and provide a realistic path back to target.

sections.heading: Stress-Test the Fund Against a Real Repair
paragraphs: The late photograph shows a mechanic working under a vehicle because “unexpected expense” should not remain abstract. Transportation can be both a repair bill and the tool that makes continued employment possible.

Choose one plausible shock from the household: vehicle repair, medical deductible, appliance replacement, home repair or one month of reduced work. Obtain a realistic range rather than inventing a round catastrophe.

[[S4|The Federal Reserve’s 2025 household survey]] reported that major vehicle repair or replacement was the most common major unexpected expense, followed by house or appliance repair and major medical costs.
Run the sequence: pay the urgent amount from the correct tier, keep priority bills funded, update remaining runway and schedule refill. Note which insurance, warranty or assistance applies.
Test a combined shock as well. A car problem can prevent work and create lost income. The fund may need to cover both repair and several days of essential burn.
Check payment logistics. Know whether the repairer accepts the account’s payment method and how quickly a savings transfer settles. Access failure can turn adequate savings into expensive borrowing.
Compare the stress test with each job profile. A remote employee may tolerate a vehicle delay; a delivery driver may lose all earnings. The same repair therefore supports different targets.
Rerun the test after changing vehicles, deductible, work location or household size. The risk model should respond to real life.
If the fund fails the test, increase the starter milestone, lower fixed burn or add appropriate insurance. Do not simply declare a larger months target without naming the gap.
The emergency fund is correctly sized when its tiers handle plausible shocks and income variability while leaving a clear path to refill—not when it matches a slogan.

Run the test with taxes and payment timing included. A repair quote may require a deposit today and a balance later, while lost work reduces the next check. Confirm whether insurance reimburses after payment and whether a rental car is necessary. The realistic cash path matters more than the final reimbursed cost.

summary: Replace a universal three- or six-month rule with a risk model based on essential burn, income variability, job concentration, replacement time, insurance, benefits and household obligations.

Calculate a lean but livable essential monthly burn from housing, utilities, food, transport, health care, childcare, insurance, minimum debt payments, taxes and essential connectivity. Convert annual costs to monthly equivalents.
Separate expense shocks from income shocks. A starter reserve can cover a deductible or repair, while income runway must cover recurring essential bills after work declines or stops.

Score income reliability using variation in hours or sales, payment delays, employer or client concentration, availability of similar work and the time needed to replace benefits. Job prestige and salary alone do not measure risk.
Dual-income households should model each lost income separately and test whether exposures are truly independent. Two jobs at the same employer or in the same industry remain concentrated.

Hourly, seasonal, commission, gig and freelance workers need cash for ordinary lean periods as well as emergencies. Keep predictable off-season money, business operating cash and tax reserves separate from household emergencies.

Adjust the target for health coverage, disability waiting periods, dependents, childcare, caregiving, licensing, mobility and geographic constraints. These factors can lengthen replacement time or increase burn.
Use three tiers: an operating buffer for timing, a starter reserve for common urgent costs, and income runway measured in months of essential burn. Keep annual bills in separate sinking funds.

Store emergency cash in a liquid, low-fee and appropriately insured account. Verify FDIC or NCUA coverage, account ownership, access time, fees and transfer limits rather than assuming every financial app is equivalent.
Balance high-rate debt against resilience. Build a starter reserve while maintaining minimums, then reduce expensive debt and redirect completed payments toward the larger runway target.

Write withdrawal rules before pressure arrives. Use the smallest suitable tier, document the event and begin a realistic refill plan after income stabilizes. Using the fund for a qualifying emergency is success.
Stress-test the target against an actual vehicle repair, medical deductible, appliance failure or reduced-income month. Include combined shocks when an expense can also interrupt work.
Review the model after job, household, insurance, housing or debt changes. Lower the target only when burn or risk truly falls, and redirect excess cash deliberately.
The correct target is explainable in dollars and risks. It protects plausible shocks without indefinitely crowding out retirement, debt reduction or other important goals.

Record the evidence behind every risk rating and review it quarterly. Employer concentration, client payment history, open roles, licensing and benefit replacement time can change. Use a target range when the facts do not support one precise number.

Model benefits separately from wages. Add replacement health premiums, deductible resets, disability waiting periods and required care to the transition budget. Dual income does not remove risk when one job carries most household benefits.

For irregular work, maintain distinct smoothing and emergency balances. Expected seasonal slowdowns use smoothing cash; exceptional illness, equipment failure or client loss uses emergency cash. This reveals whether annual pricing and income are sustainable.

Fund the tiers in order and define what happens after a withdrawal. Maintain the operating cushion, complete the starter reserve, cover near-term sinking funds and then build income runway toward the selected range.

Use quotes and payment dates in stress tests. A repair can require a deposit before insurance reimbursement and may also stop earnings. Test the cash path, not merely the final net cost after reimbursement.

For concentrated freelance or commission income, test one full delayed billing cycle. If normal obligations would consume tax money or credit, strengthen business working capital, invoice terms or client diversification before lowering the household reserve.

faq.question: Does everyone need six months of expenses?
faq.answer: No. Six months can be a useful reference, but the target should reflect essential burn, income risk, insurance and household constraints.

faq.question: Should seasonal savings count as an emergency fund?
faq.answer: No. A known off-season is predictable and should have a separate income-smoothing bucket.

faq.question: Can credit cards replace emergency savings?
faq.answer: No. Limits can change, cards can fail and borrowing creates payments during the disruption.

faq.question: Should freelancers keep business and household reserves together?
faq.answer: Track them separately so taxes and business obligations do not consume household protection.

faq.question: Where should emergency money be stored?
faq.answer: Generally in a liquid, low-fee, appropriately insured account with reliable access and strong security.

faq.question: What happens after the fund is used?
faq.answer: Recalculate runway, protect essentials and begin a sustainable refill after income stabilizes.

glossary.definition: Lean monthly cost of protected household obligations.
Checking cash for transaction timing and ordinary bill variation.
Emergency cash sized for a common urgent expense or short delay.
Liquid cash expressed as months of essential burn or monthly deficit.
Cash held for predictable low-income periods in variable work.
Savings accumulated for a known future expense.
Dependence on a small number of customers for a large share of income.
Time before an insurance or benefit payment can begin.
